title: Adaptive Preference Arithmetic: Modeling Dynamic Preference Strengths for LLM Agent Personalization (AdaPA-Agent)
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly used as personalized user assistants, effectively adapting to users' evolving preferences is critical. While user preferences are often stable in content, their relative strengths shift over time due to changing goals and contexts. Current methods face two challenges: (i) limited user feedback makes it difficult to estimate preference strengths accurately, and (ii) natural language ambiguity limits the controllability of preference-guided generation. AdaPA-Agent is an LLM-agent personalization framework that models dynamic preference strengths via Adaptive Preference Arithmetic: an alignment-based strength estimation module estimates preference strengths from existing user-agent interaction (no extra feedback), then guides controllable personalized generation by linearly combining next-token distributions weighted by the estimated strengths. Experiments on two personalization tasks - conversational recommendation and personalized web interaction - show over 18.9% and 14.2% improvements compared to ReAct.

title: Your Language Model Secretly Contains Personality Subnetworks
abstract: LLMs demonstrate flexibility in adopting different personas. Existing approaches adapt such behavior through external knowledge (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning). This work shows LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space: using small calibration datasets, distinct activation signatures associated with different personas are identified, and a masking strategy isolates lightweight persona subnetworks. A contrastive pruning strategy identifies parameters responsible for statistical divergence between binary-opposing personas (e.g., introvert-extrovert). Entirely training-free, relying solely on the existing parameter space. Resulting subnetworks exhibit significantly stronger persona alignment than baselines requiring external knowledge, while being more efficient - suggesting diverse human-like behaviors are already embedded in parameter space.

title: Interpolative Decoding: Exploring the Spectrum of Personality Traits in LLMs
abstract: To avoid creating a prompt for every tested personality profile in human-proxy simulation, this work leverages interpolative decoding: each Big Five dimension is represented as a pair of opposed prompts with an interpolation parameter to simulate behavior along the dimension. Interpolative decoding reliably modulates scores along each Big Five dimension (continuous dose control at decoding time); it causes LLMs to mimic human decision-making behavior in economic games, replicating human psychological research results; preliminary results 'twin' individual human players in a collaborative game via systematic search in interpolation space for points that replicate the human subject's actions.

title: MTI: A Behavior-Based Temperament Profiling System for AI Agents
abstract: AI models of equivalent capability can exhibit fundamentally different behavioral patterns, yet no standardized instrument measures these dispositional differences. Existing approaches borrow human personality dimensions and rely on self-report (which diverges from actual behavior in LLMs) or treat behavioral variation as a defect. The Model Temperament Index (MTI) is a behavior-based profiling system measuring AI agent temperament across four axes: Reactivity (environmental sensitivity), Compliance (instruction-behavior alignment), Sociality, and Resilience (stress resistance). MTI measures what agents do, not what they say, using structured examination protocols with a two-stage design separating capability from disposition. Profiling 10 small LMs (1.7B-9B): four axes largely independent (|r|<0.42); Compliance decomposes into independent formal/stance facets (r=0.002); Resilience into inversely related cognitive/adversarial facets; a Compliance-Resilience paradox.

title: Fusian: Multi-LoRA Fusion for Fine-Grained Continuous MBTI Personality Control in Large Language Models
abstract: Existing personality control methods (prompt engineering, standard SFT) treat personality traits as discrete categories, lacking precise control of trait intensity on a continuous spectrum. Fusian is a two-stage framework for fine-grained continuous personality control: (1) Trajectory Collection captures the dynamic evolution of personality adoption during SFT by saving a sequence of LoRA adapters, mapping the continuous manifold of a trait; (2) RL-based Dynamic Fusion trains a policy network to dynamically compute mixing weights for the frozen adapters, sampling from a Dirichlet distribution to fuse adapters and align output with a specific numerical target intensity. On Qwen3-14B, Fusian achieves high precision in aligning with user-specified trait intensities, significantly outperforming baselines.

title: Customer-R1: Personalized Simulation of Human Behaviors via RL-based LLM Agent in Online Shopping
abstract: Prior methods for step-wise human behavior simulation (prompting, SFT, RL) primarily learn a population-level policy without conditioning on a user's persona, yielding generic rather than personalized simulations. Customer-R1 is an RL-based method for personalized, step-wise user behavior simulation in online shopping environments: the policy is conditioned on an explicit persona, and next-step rationale and action generation are optimized via action correctness reward signals. On the OPeRA dataset, Customer-R1 significantly outperforms prompting and SFT-based baselines in next-action prediction, and better matches users' action distribution (higher fidelity in personalized behavior simulation).

title: Disposition Distillation at Small Scale: A Three-Arc Negative Result
abstract: Attempts to train behavioral dispositions (self-verification, uncertainty acknowledgment, feedback integration) into small LMs (0.6B-2.3B) via a four-stage distillation pipeline, inference-time attention-head interventions, and a frozen-base confidence-gated sidecar. An internal draft reported +33.9 MCAS and +15.3 HumanEval gains on Qwen3-0.6B; a sanity check falsified both (HumanEval delta was a truncation artifact inverting to -8.0; MCAS gain disappeared under apples-to-apples scoring). Across (1) SFT/DPO LoRA on three model families, (2) attention-head tempering on o_proj, (3) a training-free sidecar reading final-token hidden state h_last: no operator moves judge-measured disposition without damaging content or collapsing into stylistic mimicry, consistent across five models. Within-distribution cross-validation (AUC=0.683) collapsed to chance on fresh prompts (AUC=0.516). Contributes a two-failure-mode taxonomy for linear h_last-based approaches.

title: From Who They Are to How They Act: Behavioral Traits in Generative Agent-Based Models of Social Media
abstract: GABM frameworks characterize agents through demographic attributes, personality traits, and interests, but lack mechanisms to encode behavioral dispositions toward platform actions, causing homogeneous engagement patterns. This paper investigates behavioral traits as an explicit characterization layer to regulate agents' propensities across posting, re-sharing, commenting, reacting, and inactivity. Large-scale simulations with 980 agents validated against real-world social media data demonstrate that behavioral traits are essential to sustain heterogeneous, profile-consistent participation patterns and enable realistic content propagation via the interplay of amplification- and interaction-oriented profiles. Modeling how agents act - not only who they are - is necessary for GABM.

title: The Price of Agreement: Measuring LLM Sycophancy in Agentic Financial Applications
abstract: Evaluates sycophancy that LLMs display in agentic financial tasks. Findings: (1) models show only low to modest drops in performance in the face of user rebuttals or contradictions to the reference answer, distinguishing sycophancy in financial agentic settings from prior general-domain findings; (2) a suite of tasks tests sycophancy by user preference information contradicting the reference answer - most models fail in the presence of such inputs; (3) benchmarks different modes of recovery, such as input filtering with a pretrained LLM.

title: Agents Don't Just Agree, They Remember: Benchmarking Persistent Sycophancy in Stateful Personal Agents
abstract: Stateful personal agents maintain long-term user profiles, episodic memories, and reusable skills. This persistence turns conversational sycophancy into a state-writing failure: accepted user-centric claims can be committed as lasting preferences, background facts, or workflows and later reused after the original conversation is gone (persistent sycophancy). The Personal Agent Sycophancy Benchmark (PASB, 1,600 tasks) traces whether a claim is accepted, written into durable agent state, and reused in a later neutral query, evaluating real agents that decide what to store; it isolates the write process via four scenario framings x four temporal delivery patterns, separating a five-turn persist stage from a cleared three-turn query stage. Across twelve models the commit boundary is the key inflection point: downstream failure increases from 45.0% (session-only) to 71.9% after commitment (+27.0pp). Committed claims exhibit status promotion, attribution removal, and scope broadening, stronger under memory-like/procedural framing, repeated reinforcement, and across domain boundaries.

title: Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
abstract: LLM sycophancy poses challenges for multi-agent debating systems (MADS) that rely on productive disagreement. This work introduces the first operational framework that (1) formally defines sycophancy specific to MADS, (2) develops metrics to evaluate agent sycophancy level and its impact on information exchange, and (3) systematically investigates how varying levels of sycophancy across agent roles (debaters and judges) affects outcomes in decentralized and centralized debate frameworks. Findings: sycophancy is a core failure mode that amplifies disagreement collapse before reaching a correct conclusion, yields lower accuracy than single-agent baselines, and arises from distinct debater-driven and judge-driven failure modes. Proposes design principles balancing productive disagreement with cooperation.

title: Synthetic Socratic Debates: Examining Persona Effects on Moral Decision and Persuasion Dynamics
abstract: First large-scale study of multi-dimensional persona effects in AI-AI debates over real-world moral dilemmas. Using a 6-dimensional persona space (age, gender, country, class, ideology, personality), structured debates between AI agents are simulated over 131 relationship-based cases. Personas affect initial moral stances and debate outcomes, with political ideology and personality traits exerting the strongest influence. Persuasive success varies across traits: liberal and open personalities reach higher consensus and win rates. While logit-based confidence grows during debates, emotional and credibility-based appeals diminish, indicating more tempered argumentation over time. Trends mirror psychology/cultural-studies findings, reinforcing the need for persona-aware evaluation of AI moral reasoning.

title: Behavior-Adaptive Conversational Agents: Toward a Fluid Personality Framework
abstract: LLM-based conversational agents can project nuanced personalities and adopt diverse metaphorical roles, raising the design question: how should an agent's persona and personality be calibrated to the moment? Recent evidence suggests (i) moderate personality expression outperforms low or high extremes on trust, enjoyment, and intention to adopt in goal-oriented tasks, and (ii) context-appropriate metaphors outperform static one-note assistants on user experience and uptake. Yet most CAs fix both persona and style, risking misalignment when dynamics, urgency, and formality vary (medical information seeking, fitness coaching, reflective learning). Proposes a Fluid Personality Framework that jointly adapts (1) the agent's metaphorical persona (coach, tutor, librarian, tool) and (2) its personality expression intensity (low/medium/high) as a function of task context, user goals and traits, and situational urgency. Framework sketch with core design dimensions (no empirical system).
